title: What Is Logic?
summary: Discover what logic means, why it matters, and how logical thinking helps us reach conclusions based on evidence rather than guesses.
learningObjectives: Recognize the difference between reasoning and guessing
Identify the basic steps used in logical thinking
Explain why conclusions must be supported by information

contentBlocks.content: Logic is a disciplined way of thinking. It helps us examine information, identify relationships and reach conclusions that are supported by the available facts.

contentBlocks.title: Key idea
contentBlocks.content: Logical thinking does not ask whether an answer merely sounds believable. It asks whether the answer is properly supported by the information given.
A guess may be based on instinct, personal experience or incomplete information. A logical conclusion is reached by carefully examining the facts and applying a valid reasoning process.

contentBlocks.title: Example
contentBlocks.content: Statement: All mangoes in this basket are ripe. This fruit came from the basket. Conclusion: The fruit is ripe. The conclusion follows because it is supported by both pieces of information.

contentBlocks.title: Do not add information
contentBlocks.content: You cannot conclude that the fruit is sweet, large or yellow. Those details were not provided, even though they may be true in real life.

items: Read the information carefully.
Identify the facts that are given.
Determine what the question asks.
Avoid adding personal assumptions.
Choose the conclusion supported by the facts.

contentBlocks.title: Think about it
contentBlocks.content: A conclusion appears sensible, but one important fact required to prove it is missing. Is the conclusion logically established? No. A sensible possibility is not necessarily a valid conclusion.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson summary
contentBlocks.content: Logic helps us reach conclusions through evidence and valid reasoning. We must use the information provided, distinguish reasoning from guessing and avoid adding unstated facts.

contentBlocks.title: Key takeaways
items: Logic is disciplined and evidence-based thinking.
A valid conclusion must be supported by the given information.
A believable statement is not automatically a logical conclusion.
Never introduce facts or assumptions that the question does not provide.

title: Statements and Conclusions
summary: Learn how statements provide information and how conclusions are tested against that information.
learningObjectives: Identify conclusions supported by given information

contentBlocks.content: A statement is information provided in a reasoning question. For the purpose of answering the question, the statement must be accepted as true.

contentBlocks.title: Example of a statement
contentBlocks.content: Statement: All teachers in this school wear identity cards. This is information given by the question. You must accept it while examining any conclusion.

contentBlocks.title: Ignore outside knowledge
contentBlocks.content: Do not reject a statement because it differs from your experience. Logical reasoning questions must be answered using the information supplied in the question.
A conclusion is a result reached from the given statement or statements. A conclusion follows logically only when the information provided is sufficient to support it.

contentBlocks.title: Supported conclusion
contentBlocks.content: Statements: All roses are flowers. This plant is a rose. Conclusion: This plant is a flower. The conclusion follows because the two statements directly support it.

contentBlocks.title: The basic difference
contentBlocks.content: Statements give the information. Conclusions are the results that may be drawn from that information.

contentBlocks.title: Statement and conclusion
items: A statement is given information.
A conclusion is a result of reasoning.
Statements are accepted as true for the question.
A conclusion must be supported by the statements.
A conclusion must not introduce unsupported information.

contentBlocks.title: Check your understanding
contentBlocks.content: Statements: All buses on Route 20 stop at Central Station. Bus A travels on Route 20. Conclusion: Bus A stops at Central Station. This conclusion follows because Bus A belongs to the group described in the first statement.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson summary
contentBlocks.content: A statement provides information that must be accepted for the purpose of the question. A conclusion is valid only when it follows from that information without assumptions or outside knowledge.

contentBlocks.title: Key takeaways
items: Statements contain the given facts.
Conclusions are drawn from the given facts.
Accept the statements as true while answering.
Use only the supplied information.
Reject conclusions that require additional assumptions.

title: How to Test a Conclusion
summary: Learn a simple step-by-step method to determine whether a conclusion logically follows from the given statement without making assumptions.
learningObjectives: Understand how to test whether a conclusion follows.
Identify conclusions supported by the given statements.
Reject conclusions that require additional assumptions.
Apply a systematic method to solve Statements and Conclusions questions.

contentBlocks.content: A conclusion is accepted only when it is completely supported by the given statement or statements. Your task is not to decide whether the conclusion is true in real life, but whether it logically follows from the information provided.

items: Read every statement carefully.
Identify the important facts.
Read the proposed conclusion.
Compare the conclusion with the given facts.
Decide whether the conclusion is completely supported.

contentBlocks.title: Example 1
contentBlocks.content: Statements: All lawyers are graduates. Amal is a lawyer. Conclusion: Amal is a graduate. This conclusion follows because every lawyer is included in the group of graduates.

contentBlocks.title: Example 2
contentBlocks.content: Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red. Conclusion: All roses are red. This conclusion does not follow because the statements never say that every rose is red.

contentBlocks.title: Golden Rule
contentBlocks.content: Ask yourself: 'Can I prove this conclusion using only the given statements?' If the answer is 'No', the conclusion does not follow.

contentBlocks.title: Avoid Assumptions
contentBlocks.content: Do not use personal knowledge, experience, common sense or imagination. Use only the information given in the statements.

contentBlocks.title: Example 3
contentBlocks.content: Statement: Every employee received an identity card. Nimal is an employee. Conclusion A: Nimal received an identity card. This follows. Conclusion B: Nimal is a manager. This does not follow because the statement provides no information about his position.

contentBlocks.title: Check Your Understanding
contentBlocks.content: Statements: All bicycles have two wheels. This vehicle is a bicycle. Which conclusion follows? (A) The vehicle has two wheels. (B) The vehicle is blue. Only conclusion A follows because it is directly supported by the statements.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Summary
contentBlocks.content: A conclusion follows only when it is fully supported by the given statements. If extra information is required to prove it, the conclusion does not logically follow.

contentBlocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Read every statement carefully.
Use only the given information.
Reject conclusions requiring assumptions.
A believable conclusion is not always a logical conclusion.
Always test whether the conclusion is fully supported by the statements.
